Mujahid and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: i.e., more in agreement between hearing, sight, heart and tongue, because the sounds and movements are cut off in it. From it: "that they may make agreement with the number of what Allah has forbidden" [al-Tawbah 37], i.e., that they may agree.
al-Akhfash said: more severe in standing.
al-Farra' said: i.e., more firm for the work, and more lasting for one who wishes to increase in worship, because night is the time free from occupation with livelihood, so his worship lasts and is not cut off.
al-Kalbi said: more energetic.

﴿And more upright in speech﴾: i.e., more firm in speech and more stable in recitation, because the heart is present in it and the sounds are calm, and more upright and continuous in rightness; because the sounds in it are quiet and the world is still, so what he recites does not get confused for the one praying.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: i.e., more correct for recitation and more firm for speech, because it is a time of understanding.
Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "more upright in speech": i.e., more upright because of the freedom of mind at night.
al-Kalbi said: i.e., clearer in speech with the Qur'an.
Ikrimah said: i.e., more complete in energy and sincerity and greater in blessing.
Ibn Zayd said: more fitting that one should gain understanding of the Qur'an. It was also said: quicker in answering supplication.

﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation﴾: The majority read sabḥan with the unpointed ḥā': i.e., movement in your needs, coming and going, departing and arriving; al-sabḥ is running and circling, and from it swimming in water, because of the turning of the body and legs; and a swift horse is sābiḥ, i.e., very fast in running.
It was also said that al-sabḥ is free time: i.e., indeed you have free time by day for your needs, so pray at night.
Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., movement, coming and going in your needs and affairs.
al-Khalil said: "indeed, for you in the day is sabḥan": i.e., sleep; and al-tasabbuḥ is stretching out.
al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: if something escapes you at night, then for you by day there is free time to make up for it.
Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Wa'il and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read sabkhan with the pointed khā'. It was said the meaning of this reading is ease, spaciousness and rest.
al-Asma'i said: it is said "sabbakha Allah 'anka al-ḥummā," i.e., He lightened the fever from you; and "sabbakha al-ḥarr" means the heat abated and eased; and from it the poet's saying:
"So lighten your worry, and know that when the Most Merciful decrees something, it will be."
i.e., lighten your worry.

And tasbikh (the "sabkh" of the verse) refers to cotton that is spun after it has been carded (nadf). Al-Akhtal's verse on this is:

"They released them, scattering the dust, as the carded cotton of the bowstrings is scattered."

Tha'lab said: al-sabkh, with the unmarked kha' (sabkh), means wavering and agitation, and al-sabkh also means stillness.

Abu 'Amr said: al-sabkh means sleep and leisure.

﴿And remember the name of your Lord﴾: that is, call upon Him by His most beautiful names. It was also said: recite "in the name of your Lord" at the beginning of your prayer. It was also said: remember the name of your Lord in His promise and His threat, so that you may be keen in obedience to Him and keep far from disobeying Him. It was also said that the meaning is: persist in remembering your Lord by night and by day, and increase in that.

Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is, pray to your Lord, ﴿and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾, that is, sever yourself toward Him by devoting yourself to His worship. Tabattul means severance. One says "I battalt the thing," meaning I cut it off and separated it from other things. A "batlah" charity is one cut off from the property of its owner. A monk is called "mutabattil" because he is severed from people. On this, the poet says:

"She lights up the darkness at nightfall, as if she were
the lamp of an evening-monk, a devoted hermit."

[The verse uses] "tabtil" in place of "tabattul" for the sake of the rhyme of the verse-endings (fawasil).

Al-Wahidi said: tabattul is the renunciation of this world and all that is in it, and the seeking of what is with Allah.

﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir read "Rabb" in the genitive (jarr), as an adjective (na't) of "Rabbika," or a substitute (badal) for it, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it.

The rest read it in the nominative (raf'), either as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Lord of the East.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the accusative (nasb), as praise (mad-h).

The majority read ﴿al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib﴾ in the singular dual form, while Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb" in the plural. We have already explained the meaning of "al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib," and of "al-mashriqayn wa-l-maghribayn" and "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb."

﴿So take Him as your trustee (wakil)﴾: that is, once you know that He alone is the One specialized in lordship, then take Him as your trustee, meaning one who manages your affairs, and rely upon Him in all of them. It was also said: take Him as your guarantor (kafil) for what He has promised you of reward and victory.

﴿And be patient over what they say﴾: of harm, abuse, and mockery, and do not be distressed by that. ﴿And keep away from them with gracious aversion﴾: that is, do not confront them, and do not occupy yourself with repaying them. It was also said that "gracious aversion" (al-hajr al-jamil) is that in which there is no distress. This was before the command to fight.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾: that is, leave them to Me, and do not concern yourself with them, for I will suffice you in their affair and take vengeance on them on your behalf.

It was said that this was revealed concerning the feeders (al-mut'imun) on the day of Badr, who were ten, and their mention has already passed.

Yahya ibn Salam said: they are the sons of al-Mughirah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: I was told they were twelve.

﴿Possessors of luxury﴾: that is, the wealthy, those of abundance, ease, and enjoyment of pleasure in this world. ﴿And give them respite a little﴾: that is, a little respite, taken as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a little time, taken as an adjective of an omitted time-noun (zaman). The meaning: give them respite until the end of their terms. It was also said: until the descent of the punishment of this world upon them, as on the day of Badr.

The first is preferable, because of His saying ﴿Indeed with Us are shackles﴾ and what follows it, for it is a threat to them of the punishment of the Hereafter. Ankal is the plural of nakl, which is a fetter. So said al-Hasan, Mujahid and others. Al-Kalbi said: al-ankal are shackles (aghlal). The first is better known in the language. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"They came to you, and their shackles were cut,
though before you they had never been cut."

Muqatil said: they are kinds of severe punishment.

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: they are fetters that cannot be undone, and a blazing fire (jahim), that is, a kindled fire.

﴿And food that chokes﴾: that is, it does not go down the throat, but lodges in it, so it neither goes down nor comes out.

Mujahid said: it is the zaqqum.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is the dari' (a thorny plant), as He said: ﴿They have no food except from dari'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. He said: it is the thorn of the 'awsaj (a thorny shrub).

'Ikrimah said: it is a thorn that catches in the throat, neither going in nor coming out. The ghussah is the bone (shaja) in the throat, which is what lodges in it, of bone or something else, and its plural is ghusas. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾: that is, another kind of punishment, other than what has been mentioned.

﴿On the day the earth and the mountains quake﴾: the accusative of the time-phrase (zarf) is either governed by "dharni" (leave Me), or by the "being established" (istiqrar) that is related to "ladayna" (with Us), or it is an adjective of "'adhaban" (punishment), so it is attached to an omitted element: that is, a punishment occurring on the day of quaking; or it is attached to "alimam" (painful).

The majority read "turjifu" with a fatha on the ta' and damma on the jim, in the active voice. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the passive voice, derived from "arjafaha" (he made it quake), and the meaning is: it shakes and convulses with those upon it. Al-rajfah is the earthquake and the violent trembling.

﴿And the mountains will be a heap of sand, poured out﴾: that is, and the mountains will be. He expressed it in the past tense because of the certainty of its occurrence. Kathib is the gathered sand, and mahil is that which passes beneath the feet.

Al-Wahidi said: that is, flowing sand. It is said of anything you release as dust or food, "ahaltuhu hailan" (I poured it out).

Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: mahil is that which, when you step on it with the foot, slips away beneath it, and when you take its base, it collapses. On this, Hassan says:

"I recognized the abodes of Zaynab in the sand-heap,
like the writing of revelation on fresh paper."

﴿Indeed We have sent to you a messenger, a witness over you﴾: the address is to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to all disbelievers. The messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning: he will bear witness against you on the Day of Resurrection concerning your deeds. ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾: meaning Musa.

﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ whom We had sent to him, and he denied him and did not believe in what he brought. The place (mahall) of the kaf (as) is accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The meaning: Indeed We sent to you a messenger, and you disobeyed him, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger, and he disobeyed him.

﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizure﴾: that is, severe, heavy, and harsh. The meaning: We punished Pharaoh with a severe and harsh punishment by drowning. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah, that the same kind of punishment that came upon him will come upon them, even though the type of punishment differs.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, heavy and harsh; from this, rain is called "wabil" (heavy rain).

Al-Akhfash said: severe. The meanings are close. From it comes "ta'am wabil" (heavy food), meaning food that is not digestible. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"Bujaylah ate, on the day they met
the knights of Malik, a heavy eating."

﴿Then how will you guard yourselves﴾: that is, how will you protect yourselves if you disbelieve, that is, if you remain upon your disbelief, on a day, that is, the punishment of a day ﴿that will make children grey-haired﴾, because of its terrible severity. That is, the children will become old men. Shayb is the plural of ashyab. This may be literal, that they will actually become so, or figurative, because whoever witnesses a great terror has his strength diminished, his limbs weakened, and becomes like an old man in weakness and loss of power. In this there is a severe rebuke for them and a great reproach.

Al-Hasan said: that is, how will you guard yourselves against a day that will make children grey-haired if you disbelieve? Ibn Mas'ud and 'Atiyyah also read it so, with "yawman" as an object (maf'ul bih) of "tattaqun" (you guard against).

Ibn al-Anbari said: some have put "al-yawm" in the accusative governed by "kafartum" (you disbelieved), but this is ugly (qabih).

"Al-wildan" means the children.

Then He increased the description of that day in severity, saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder thereby﴾: that is, split open by it because of its severity and great terror. The clause is another adjective of "yawm." The ba' is causal (sababiyyah). It was said it means "in," that is, splitting open in it; and it was said it means "for," that is, splitting open for it. He said "munfatir" and not "munfatirah" (feminine) because the heaven is treated as a thing, since it has changed, and nothing remains of it except what is expressed as "a thing."

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: He did not say "munfatirah" because its figurative meaning (majaz) is the roof, as the poet said:

"Even if a people were raised to it (the heaven),
we would reach the heaven and the clouds."

So this is like His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected roof﴾.

Al-Farra' said: the heaven is both masculine and feminine.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is of the type of "scattered locusts" and "green tree," and [of the verse] ﴿trunks of uprooted palms﴾ [al-Qamar: 20]. He also said: that is, the heaven possesses splitting, like their saying "a woman who is murdid (nursing)": that is, one possessed of nursing, by way of attribution. Its splitting is for the descent of the angels, as He said: ﴿When the heaven is split apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], and His saying: ﴿The heavens are about to be split open from above them﴾.

It was also said "munfatir bihi" means: by Allah, and the intended meaning is by His command. The first is preferable.

﴿His promise was ever fulfilled﴾: that is, the promise of Allah regarding what He promised of resurrection, reckoning, and other things, was certain to occur without doubt. The verbal noun (masdar) is then attached to its agent (fa'il). Or it means: the promise of the day was fulfilled, and then the verbal noun is attached to its object (maf'ul).

Muqatil said: His promise was that He would make His religion prevail over all religion.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Muhammad ibn Nasr in the Book of Prayer, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Sa'd ibn Hisham, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: Tell me about the night prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: Do you not recite this surah, 'O you who wraps himself' (al-Muzzammil)? I said: Yes. She said: Indeed Allah made the night prayer obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions stood in prayer for a year, until their feet swelled. And Allah held back its conclusion in the heaven for twelve months. Then He sent down the relief at the end of this surah, and the night prayer became voluntary after it had been obligatory."

This hadith has been related from her through several chains.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the beginning of al-Muzzammil was revealed, they used to stand in prayer about as much as they stood in Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and there was about a year between its beginning and its end.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Nasr have related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: When "O you who wraps himself" was revealed, they stood for a year until their feet and shins swelled, until ﴿so recite what is easy of it﴾ was revealed, and the people rested.

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh (book on abrogation, naskh), Ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Concerning al-Muzzammil, ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night, except a little, half of it﴾ was abrogated (nasakhat) by the verse in which is ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness; so recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾. And "nashi'at al-layl" is its beginning. Their prayer was at the beginning of the night. He says: this is more likely to make you keep count of what Allah has obligated upon you of the night prayer, because when a person sleeps he does not know when he will wake up. As for His saying: ﴿more upright in speech﴾, it is more likely to enable one to understand the recitation of the Qur'an. And His saying: ﴿Indeed for you in the day is a long occupation (sabh)﴾ means a long leisure.

Al-Hakim (who authenticated it) has related from him concerning His saying "O you who wraps himself": he said: I wrapped myself in this matter, so stand up to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir has related from him, concerning the same verse, that he said: he wraps himself in garments.

Al-Firyabi has related from Abu Salih from him, concerning ﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation (tartil)﴾, that he said: you recite two verses, three, then you pause, without rushing (la tuhdir).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mani' in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Muhammad ibn Nasr have related from him also, concerning ﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation﴾, that he said: make it clear with clear articulation.

al-'Askari in al-Mawa'iz has related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Nasr, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from 'A'ishah that "when revelation came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on his she-camel, she would lower her chest (jiran), and she could not move until he was relieved of it. And she recited: ﴿Indeed We will convey to you a weighty word﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night (nashi'ata al-layl)﴾, that he said: standing in prayer at night, in the language of Abyssinia, when a man stands up, they say "nasha'a" (he has risen).

al-Bayhaqi has related from him, who said: "nashi'at al-layl" is its beginning.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Nasr have related from him also, who said: the whole night is "nashi'ah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "nashi'at al-layl," in Abyssinian, is the standing in prayer at night.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in al-Musannaf (the compiled collection), and Ibn Nasr and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: ﴿The rising of the night﴾ is what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim in al-Kuna reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, for you by day there is a long occupation﴾, that he said: "Al-sabh (the free time) is leisure for need and for sleep."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, the Proofs of Prophethood), reported from Aisha, who said: When there was revealed ﴿Leave Me with those who deny, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾, it was not long before the Battle of Badr occurred.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾, that he said: "Shackles (quyud)."

Abd ibn Humayd, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd (the additions to the Book of Asceticism), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And food that chokes﴾, that he said: "It is the tree of al-Zaqqum."

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from him regarding His words ﴿a heap of sand, collapsing﴾, that he said: "The collapsing (al-mahil) is that which, when you take some of it, its remainder follows you down."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: regarding ﴿a heap of sand, collapsing﴾, he said: "The flowing sand." And regarding His words ﴿a severe seizing﴾, he said: "Severe."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited ﴿that will make the children grey-haired﴾ and said: "That is the Day of Resurrection, the day when Allah says to Adam: 'Stand up and send forth from your offspring a company to the Fire.' He said: 'From how many, O Lord?' He said: 'From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine, and one will be saved.' This was hard on the Muslims, and when he saw that in their faces he said: 'Indeed, the children of Adam are many, and Ya'juj and Ma'juj are from the offspring of Adam. Indeed, no man of them dies until there is born to him from his loins a thousand men. So among them and their likes is a shield for you.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar to it, but more concise.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the chain of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿the sky splitting asunder by it﴾, that he said: "Filled with the tongue of Abyssinia."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "Heavy, burdened."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding this verse that he said: "It means the cracking of the sky."

It is a Meccan surah.
Al-Mawardi said: all of it is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir. He said: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except two verses from it, "﴿And bear patiently what they say﴾" and the one that follows it.
Al-Tha'labi said: except His saying: "﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer]...﴾" to the end of the surah, for it was revealed at Medina.
Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed at Mecca."
Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Nahhas related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of al-Muzzammil was revealed at Mecca, except two verses: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night...﴾"
Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il related from Jabir, who said: "The Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwa and said: 'Give this man a name by which you will turn people away from him.' They said: 'He is a soothsayer.' They said: 'He is not a soothsayer.' They said: 'He is a madman.' They said: 'He is not a madman.' They said: 'He is a sorcerer.' They said: 'He is not a sorcerer.' So the polytheists dispersed over that."
The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself with them. Then Jibril came to him and said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿O you who are covered﴾" [i.e., the surah of al-Muddaththir].
Al-Bazzar said, after relating it through the route of Mu'alla ibn Abd al-Rahman: "Mu'alla has been narrated from by a group of people of knowledge and they accepted his narrations, but when he alone transmits hadiths, they are not followed in them."
Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I spent the night with my maternal aunt Maymunah. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray at night, and he prayed thirteen rak'ahs, among them the two rak'ahs of Fajr. I estimated his standing in each rak'ah to be about the length of [reciting] ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ — its origin is al-mutazammil, so the ta' is assimilated into the zay, and tazammul means wrapping oneself in a garment.
The majority read al-muzzammil with assimilation (idgham).
Ubayy read al-mutazammil, in its original form.
Ikrimah read it with the zay lightened, and a line like this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"As if Thabir, in the folds of its rain-clouds, were an old man wrapped in a cave-dwelling."
This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and its meaning has been disputed.
A group said: he (ﷺ) used to wrap himself in his garments at the beginning, when Jibril brought him the revelation, out of fear, until he became at ease with it. It was also said the meaning is: O you who are wrapped up with prophethood, and committed to the message.
Ikrimah said this, and he used to read "yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil" with the zay lightened and the mim with a fatha and shadda, as a passive participle. It was also said the meaning is: O you who are wrapped up in the Qur'an.
Al-Dahhak said: he wrapped himself in his garments for sleep. It was also said: word of harm from the polytheists reached him, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself, and then ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ and ﴿O you who are covered﴾ were revealed.
It is established that when the Prophet (ﷺ) heard the voice of the angel and looked at him, trembling seized him, and he came to his family and said: "Wrap me up, cover me up!" His address (ﷺ) with this form was at the beginning of the revelation's descent.
After that he was addressed with prophethood and the message.

﴿Stand [in prayer] during the night, except a little﴾: i.e., stand up for prayer at night.
The majority read qum with a kasra on the mim, due to the meeting of two sukuns.
Abu al-Simmak read it with a damma, following the damma of the qaf.
Uthman ibn Jinni said: the purpose of this vowel is to avoid the meeting of two sukuns, so whichever vowel you move it with, the purpose is achieved.
The accusative of al-layl (the night) is as an adverb of time.
It was also said that the meaning of qum is ṣalli (pray), expressed by it and used metaphorically for it.
It has been disputed whether this standing he was commanded to was obligatory for him or voluntary; what has been reported on that will come, God willing.
His saying: "except a little" is an exception from "the night": i.e., pray the whole night except a small part of it. "A little" of a thing is what is less than half; it was also said less than a sixth; it was also said less than a tenth.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: what is meant by "a little" here is a third.
This disagreement is made unnecessary by His saying: "half of it" etc. The accusative of "half of it" is as a substitute (badal) for "the night".
Al-Zajjaj said: "half of it" is a substitute for "the night", and "except a little" is an exception from "the half", and the pronoun in "from it" and "upon it" refers to the half.
The meaning: stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little to a third, or add to it a little to two-thirds; so it is as if he said: stand two-thirds of the night, or its half, or its third.
It was also said that "half of it" is a substitute for "a little". Then the meaning would be: stand the night except half of it, or less than half of it, or more than half of it. Al-Akhfash said: "half of it" means "or half of it", just as one says: give him a dirham, two dirhams, three, meaning "or two dirhams, or three."
Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: reduce from the half a little to a third, or add to the half up to two-thirds. He was given latitude in the duration of his standing in the night and was given the choice of these periods for standing. The Prophet (ﷺ) and a group with him used to stand in these measures, and it was hard on them, so a man did not know how much he had prayed or how much of the night remained, and he would stand the whole night, until Allah lightened it for them.
It was also said that the two pronouns in "from it" and "upon it" refer to the lesser part of the half, as if he said: stand less than half of it, or stand less than that lesser part, or slightly more than it. This is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that "half of it" is a substitute for "a little", and the two pronouns refer to the half that is substituted for "a little".
The abrogating element of this command has been disputed. It was said it is His saying: "Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it" to the end of the surah. It was said it is His saying: "He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it." It was said it is His saying: "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill." It was said it is abrogated by the five daily prayers; this was said by Muqatil, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Kaysan. It was said it is His saying: "So recite what is easy of it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin held that night prayer is obligatory on every Muslim, even the amount of milking a sheep.

﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured tones﴾: i.e., recite it slowly, with reflection.
Al-Dahhak said: recite it letter by letter.
Al-Zajjaj said: it is that one makes clear all the letters and gives each its due extension.
The origin of tartil is arrangement, orderliness and good sequence; and emphasizing the verb with the verbal noun indicates intensity, in a manner in which some letters are not confused with others, and nothing is lost from the pronunciation of a letter from its known point of articulation, while fully observing its prescribed vowel.

﴿Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word﴾: i.e., We will reveal to you the Qur'an, which is a weighty word.
Qatadah said: by Allah, weighty are its obligations and its limits.
Mujahid said: its lawful and its unlawful.
Al-Hasan said: acting upon it.
Abu al-Aliyah said: weighty with the promise and the threat, and the lawful and the unlawful.
Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "weighty" in the sense of noble, from the saying "so-and-so is weighty upon me," i.e., he is honored by me.
Al-Farra' said: weighty, firm, not light and trivial, because it is the speech of our Lord.
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: weighty, which none can bear except a heart supported by success and a soul adorned with monotheism. It was also said that describing it as weighty is literal, because it is established that when the Prophet (ﷺ) received revelation while on his she-camel, she would lay her chest on the ground and could not move until it had passed from him.

﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾: i.e., its hours and its times, because they arise one after another. It is said: "the thing arose" (nasha'a yansha'u) when it began and came one thing after another, so it is nashi'; and Allah brought it into being and it arose; from it: "the clouds arose" when they began. So nashi'ah is the feminine active participle of nasha'a yansha'u, so it is nashi'ah.
Al-Zajjaj said: the rising of the night is every part of it that arises, i.e., comes into being; so it is nashi'ah. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: the whole night is nashi'ah, and what is meant is that the hours of the night are the arising ones, so the descriptive is used in place of the noun described.
It was also said that the rising of the night is the soul that rises from its bed to worship, i.e., gets up, from "nasha'a min makanihi" when he rose from his place.
It was said: "nashi'ah" in Abyssinian means the standing at night. It was also said: the term nā'ishah for the standing at night is used only when it is after sleep.
Ibn al-A'rabi said: if you sleep from the beginning of the night and then rise, that is al-munsha'ah and al-nash'ah, and from it "rising of the night."
It was also said: the rising of the night is what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha', because the meaning of nasha'a is "began," and from it is the saying of Nusayb:
"Were it not that it would be said that Nusayb is childish, I would have said: 'I give myself for the young children (al-nash')'."
Ikrimah and Ata' said: the rising of the night is the beginning of the night.
Mujahid and others said: it is in the whole night, because it arises after the day; Malik chose this.
Ibn Kaysan said: it is standing at the end of the night.
Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: nā'ishat al-layl is the first of its hours.
Al-Hasan said: it is what comes after the late 'Isha' until dawn.

﴿It is more severe in treading﴾: The majority read wath'an with a fatha on the waw and sukun on the ta', maqsura (short-vowelled). Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Mujahid, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Mughirah and Abu Haywah read wiṭ'an with a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ta', mamdud (long). Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading.
So the meaning according to the first reading is that prayer during the rising of the night is heavier on the one who prays than prayer during the day, because the night is for sleep.
Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that it is heavier on the one who prays than the hours of the day, from the Arabs' saying: "the authority's trampling (wiṭ'at al-sultan) was severe on the people," when what is required of them from it became heavy upon them; and from it His saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, make your trampling heavy upon Mudar."
The meaning according to the second reading is that it is more conducive to agreement (muwāṭa'ah), i.e., more in accord, from the saying: "I agreed with so-and-so upon such-and-such, muwāṭa'ah and wiṭā'," when I concurred with him upon it.
Mujahid and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: i.e., more in agreement between hearing, sight, heart and tongue, because the sounds and movements are cut off in it. From it: "that they may make agreement with the number of what Allah has forbidden" [al-Tawbah 37], i.e., that they may agree.
al-Akhfash said: more severe in standing.
al-Farra' said: i.e., more firm for the work, and more lasting for one who wishes to increase in worship, because night is the time free from occupation with livelihood, so his worship lasts and is not cut off.
al-Kalbi said: more energetic.

﴿And more upright in speech﴾: i.e., more firm in speech and more stable in recitation, because the heart is present in it and the sounds are calm, and more upright and continuous in rightness; because the sounds in it are quiet and the world is still, so what he recites does not get confused for the one praying.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: i.e., more correct for recitation and more firm for speech, because it is a time of understanding.
Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "more upright in speech": i.e., more upright because of the freedom of mind at night.
al-Kalbi said: i.e., clearer in speech with the Qur'an.
Ikrimah said: i.e., more complete in energy and sincerity and greater in blessing.
Ibn Zayd said: more fitting that one should gain understanding of the Qur'an. It was also said: quicker in answering supplication.

﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation﴾: The majority read sabḥan with the unpointed ḥā': i.e., movement in your needs, coming and going, departing and arriving; al-sabḥ is running and circling, and from it swimming in water, because of the turning of the body and legs; and a swift horse is sābiḥ, i.e., very fast in running.
It was also said that al-sabḥ is free time: i.e., indeed you have free time by day for your needs, so pray at night.
Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., movement, coming and going in your needs and affairs.
al-Khalil said: "indeed, for you in the day is sabḥan": i.e., sleep; and al-tasabbuḥ is stretching out.
al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: if something escapes you at night, then for you by day there is free time to make up for it.
Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Wa'il and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read sabkhan with the pointed khā'. It was said the meaning of this reading is ease, spaciousness and rest.
al-Asma'i said: it is said "sabbakha Allah 'anka al-ḥummā," i.e., He lightened the fever from you; and "sabbakha al-ḥarr" means the heat abated and eased; and from it the poet's saying:
"So lighten your worry, and know that when the Most Merciful decrees something, it will be."
i.e., lighten your worry.

And tasbikh (the "sabkh" of the verse) refers to cotton that is spun after it has been carded (nadf). Al-Akhtal's verse on this is:

"They released them, scattering the dust, as the carded cotton of the bowstrings is scattered."

Tha'lab said: al-sabkh, with the unmarked kha' (sabkh), means wavering and agitation, and al-sabkh also means stillness.

Abu 'Amr said: al-sabkh means sleep and leisure.

﴿And remember the name of your Lord﴾: that is, call upon Him by His most beautiful names. It was also said: recite "in the name of your Lord" at the beginning of your prayer. It was also said: remember the name of your Lord in His promise and His threat, so that you may be keen in obedience to Him and keep far from disobeying Him. It was also said that the meaning is: persist in remembering your Lord by night and by day, and increase in that.

Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is, pray to your Lord, ﴿and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾, that is, sever yourself toward Him by devoting yourself to His worship. Tabattul means severance. One says "I battalt the thing," meaning I cut it off and separated it from other things. A "batlah" charity is one cut off from the property of its owner. A monk is called "mutabattil" because he is severed from people. On this, the poet says:

"She lights up the darkness at nightfall, as if she were
the lamp of an evening-monk, a devoted hermit."

[The verse uses] "tabtil" in place of "tabattul" for the sake of the rhyme of the verse-endings (fawasil).

Al-Wahidi said: tabattul is the renunciation of this world and all that is in it, and the seeking of what is with Allah.

﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir read "Rabb" in the genitive (jarr), as an adjective (na't) of "Rabbika," or a substitute (badal) for it, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it.

The rest read it in the nominative (raf'), either as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Lord of the East.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the accusative (nasb), as praise (mad-h).

The majority read ﴿al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib﴾ in the singular dual form, while Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb" in the plural. We have already explained the meaning of "al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib," and of "al-mashriqayn wa-l-maghribayn" and "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb."

﴿So take Him as your trustee (wakil)﴾: that is, once you know that He alone is the One specialized in lordship, then take Him as your trustee, meaning one who manages your affairs, and rely upon Him in all of them. It was also said: take Him as your guarantor (kafil) for what He has promised you of reward and victory.

﴿And be patient over what they say﴾: of harm, abuse, and mockery, and do not be distressed by that. ﴿And keep away from them with gracious aversion﴾: that is, do not confront them, and do not occupy yourself with repaying them. It was also said that "gracious aversion" (al-hajr al-jamil) is that in which there is no distress. This was before the command to fight.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾: that is, leave them to Me, and do not concern yourself with them, for I will suffice you in their affair and take vengeance on them on your behalf.

It was said that this was revealed concerning the feeders (al-mut'imun) on the day of Badr, who were ten, and their mention has already passed.

Yahya ibn Salam said: they are the sons of al-Mughirah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: I was told they were twelve.

﴿Possessors of luxury﴾: that is, the wealthy, those of abundance, ease, and enjoyment of pleasure in this world. ﴿And give them respite a little﴾: that is, a little respite, taken as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a little time, taken as an adjective of an omitted time-noun (zaman). The meaning: give them respite until the end of their terms. It was also said: until the descent of the punishment of this world upon them, as on the day of Badr.

The first is preferable, because of His saying ﴿Indeed with Us are shackles﴾ and what follows it, for it is a threat to them of the punishment of the Hereafter. Ankal is the plural of nakl, which is a fetter. So said al-Hasan, Mujahid and others. Al-Kalbi said: al-ankal are shackles (aghlal). The first is better known in the language. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"They came to you, and their shackles were cut,
though before you they had never been cut."

Muqatil said: they are kinds of severe punishment.

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: they are fetters that cannot be undone, and a blazing fire (jahim), that is, a kindled fire.

﴿And food that chokes﴾: that is, it does not go down the throat, but lodges in it, so it neither goes down nor comes out.

Mujahid said: it is the zaqqum.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is the dari' (a thorny plant), as He said: ﴿They have no food except from dari'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. He said: it is the thorn of the 'awsaj (a thorny shrub).

'Ikrimah said: it is a thorn that catches in the throat, neither going in nor coming out. The ghussah is the bone (shaja) in the throat, which is what lodges in it, of bone or something else, and its plural is ghusas. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾: that is, another kind of punishment, other than what has been mentioned.

﴿On the day the earth and the mountains quake﴾: the accusative of the time-phrase (zarf) is either governed by "dharni" (leave Me), or by the "being established" (istiqrar) that is related to "ladayna" (with Us), or it is an adjective of "'adhaban" (punishment), so it is attached to an omitted element: that is, a punishment occurring on the day of quaking; or it is attached to "alimam" (painful).

The majority read "turjifu" with a fatha on the ta' and damma on the jim, in the active voice. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the passive voice, derived from "arjafaha" (he made it quake), and the meaning is: it shakes and convulses with those upon it. Al-rajfah is the earthquake and the violent trembling.

﴿And the mountains will be a heap of sand, poured out﴾: that is, and the mountains will be. He expressed it in the past tense because of the certainty of its occurrence. Kathib is the gathered sand, and mahil is that which passes beneath the feet.

Al-Wahidi said: that is, flowing sand. It is said of anything you release as dust or food, "ahaltuhu hailan" (I poured it out).

Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: mahil is that which, when you step on it with the foot, slips away beneath it, and when you take its base, it collapses. On this, Hassan says:

"I recognized the abodes of Zaynab in the sand-heap,
like the writing of revelation on fresh paper."

﴿Indeed We have sent to you a messenger, a witness over you﴾: the address is to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to all disbelievers. The messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning: he will bear witness against you on the Day of Resurrection concerning your deeds. ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾: meaning Musa.

﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ whom We had sent to him, and he denied him and did not believe in what he brought. The place (mahall) of the kaf (as) is accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The meaning: Indeed We sent to you a messenger, and you disobeyed him, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger, and he disobeyed him.

﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizure﴾: that is, severe, heavy, and harsh. The meaning: We punished Pharaoh with a severe and harsh punishment by drowning. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah, that the same kind of punishment that came upon him will come upon them, even though the type of punishment differs.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, heavy and harsh; from this, rain is called "wabil" (heavy rain).

Al-Akhfash said: severe. The meanings are close. From it comes "ta'am wabil" (heavy food), meaning food that is not digestible. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"Bujaylah ate, on the day they met
the knights of Malik, a heavy eating."

﴿Then how will you guard yourselves﴾: that is, how will you protect yourselves if you disbelieve, that is, if you remain upon your disbelief, on a day, that is, the punishment of a day ﴿that will make children grey-haired﴾, because of its terrible severity. That is, the children will become old men. Shayb is the plural of ashyab. This may be literal, that they will actually become so, or figurative, because whoever witnesses a great terror has his strength diminished, his limbs weakened, and becomes like an old man in weakness and loss of power. In this there is a severe rebuke for them and a great reproach.

Al-Hasan said: that is, how will you guard yourselves against a day that will make children grey-haired if you disbelieve? Ibn Mas'ud and 'Atiyyah also read it so, with "yawman" as an object (maf'ul bih) of "tattaqun" (you guard against).

Ibn al-Anbari said: some have put "al-yawm" in the accusative governed by "kafartum" (you disbelieved), but this is ugly (qabih).

"Al-wildan" means the children.

Then He increased the description of that day in severity, saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder thereby﴾: that is, split open by it because of its severity and great terror. The clause is another adjective of "yawm." The ba' is causal (sababiyyah). It was said it means "in," that is, splitting open in it; and it was said it means "for," that is, splitting open for it. He said "munfatir" and not "munfatirah" (feminine) because the heaven is treated as a thing, since it has changed, and nothing remains of it except what is expressed as "a thing."

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: He did not say "munfatirah" because its figurative meaning (majaz) is the roof, as the poet said:

"Even if a people were raised to it (the heaven),
we would reach the heaven and the clouds."

So this is like His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected roof﴾.

Al-Farra' said: the heaven is both masculine and feminine.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is of the type of "scattered locusts" and "green tree," and [of the verse] ﴿trunks of uprooted palms﴾ [al-Qamar: 20]. He also said: that is, the heaven possesses splitting, like their saying "a woman who is murdid (nursing)": that is, one possessed of nursing, by way of attribution. Its splitting is for the descent of the angels, as He said: ﴿When the heaven is split apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], and His saying: ﴿The heavens are about to be split open from above them﴾.

It was also said "munfatir bihi" means: by Allah, and the intended meaning is by His command. The first is preferable.

﴿His promise was ever fulfilled﴾: that is, the promise of Allah regarding what He promised of resurrection, reckoning, and other things, was certain to occur without doubt. The verbal noun (masdar) is then attached to its agent (fa'il). Or it means: the promise of the day was fulfilled, and then the verbal noun is attached to its object (maf'ul).

Muqatil said: His promise was that He would make His religion prevail over all religion.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Muhammad ibn Nasr in the Book of Prayer, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Sa'd ibn Hisham, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: Tell me about the night prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: Do you not recite this surah, 'O you who wraps himself' (al-Muzzammil)? I said: Yes. She said: Indeed Allah made the night prayer obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions stood in prayer for a year, until their feet swelled. And Allah held back its conclusion in the heaven for twelve months. Then He sent down the relief at the end of this surah, and the night prayer became voluntary after it had been obligatory."

This hadith has been related from her through several chains.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the beginning of al-Muzzammil was revealed, they used to stand in prayer about as much as they stood in Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and there was about a year between its beginning and its end.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Nasr have related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: When "O you who wraps himself" was revealed, they stood for a year until their feet and shins swelled, until ﴿so recite what is easy of it﴾ was revealed, and the people rested.

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh (book on abrogation, naskh), Ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Concerning al-Muzzammil, ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night, except a little, half of it﴾ was abrogated (nasakhat) by the verse in which is ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness; so recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾. And "nashi'at al-layl" is its beginning. Their prayer was at the beginning of the night. He says: this is more likely to make you keep count of what Allah has obligated upon you of the night prayer, because when a person sleeps he does not know when he will wake up. As for His saying: ﴿more upright in speech﴾, it is more likely to enable one to understand the recitation of the Qur'an. And His saying: ﴿Indeed for you in the day is a long occupation (sabh)﴾ means a long leisure.

Al-Hakim (who authenticated it) has related from him concerning His saying "O you who wraps himself": he said: I wrapped myself in this matter, so stand up to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir has related from him, concerning the same verse, that he said: he wraps himself in garments.

Al-Firyabi has related from Abu Salih from him, concerning ﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation (tartil)﴾, that he said: you recite two verses, three, then you pause, without rushing (la tuhdir).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mani' in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Muhammad ibn Nasr have related from him also, concerning ﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation﴾, that he said: make it clear with clear articulation.

al-'Askari in al-Mawa'iz has related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Nasr, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from 'A'ishah that "when revelation came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on his she-camel, she would lower her chest (jiran), and she could not move until he was relieved of it. And she recited: ﴿Indeed We will convey to you a weighty word﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night (nashi'ata al-layl)﴾, that he said: standing in prayer at night, in the language of Abyssinia, when a man stands up, they say "nasha'a" (he has risen).

al-Bayhaqi has related from him, who said: "nashi'at al-layl" is its beginning.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Nasr have related from him also, who said: the whole night is "nashi'ah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "nashi'at al-layl," in Abyssinian, is the standing in prayer at night.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in al-Musannaf (the compiled collection), and Ibn Nasr and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: ﴿The rising of the night﴾ is what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim in al-Kuna reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, for you by day there is a long occupation﴾, that he said: "Al-sabh (the free time) is leisure for need and for sleep."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, the Proofs of Prophethood), reported from Aisha, who said: When there was revealed ﴿Leave Me with those who deny, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾, it was not long before the Battle of Badr occurred.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾, that he said: "Shackles (quyud)."

Abd ibn Humayd, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd (the additions to the Book of Asceticism), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And food that chokes﴾, that he said: "It is the tree of al-Zaqqum."

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from him regarding His words ﴿a heap of sand, collapsing﴾, that he said: "The collapsing (al-mahil) is that which, when you take some of it, its remainder follows you down."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: regarding ﴿a heap of sand, collapsing﴾, he said: "The flowing sand." And regarding His words ﴿a severe seizing﴾, he said: "Severe."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him also that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited ﴿that will make the children grey-haired﴾ and said: "That is the Day of Resurrection, the day when Allah says to Adam: 'Stand up and send forth from your offspring a company to the Fire.' He said: 'From how many, O Lord?' He said: 'From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine, and one will be saved.' This was hard on the Muslims, and when he saw that in their faces he said: 'Indeed, the children of Adam are many, and Ya'juj and Ma'juj are from the offspring of Adam. Indeed, no man of them dies until there is born to him from his loins a thousand men. So among them and their likes is a shield for you.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar to it, but more concise.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the chain of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿the sky splitting asunder by it﴾, that he said: "Filled with the tongue of Abyssinia."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "Heavy, burdened."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding this verse that he said: "It means the cracking of the sky."

It is a Meccan surah.
Al-Mawardi said: all of it is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir. He said: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except two verses from it, "﴿And bear patiently what they say﴾" and the one that follows it.
Al-Tha'labi said: except His saying: "﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer]...﴾" to the end of the surah, for it was revealed at Medina.
Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed at Mecca."
Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Nahhas related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of al-Muzzammil was revealed at Mecca, except two verses: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night...﴾"
Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il related from Jabir, who said: "The Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwa and said: 'Give this man a name by which you will turn people away from him.' They said: 'He is a soothsayer.' They said: 'He is not a soothsayer.' They said: 'He is a madman.' They said: 'He is not a madman.' They said: 'He is a sorcerer.' They said: 'He is not a sorcerer.' So the polytheists dispersed over that."
The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself with them. Then Jibril came to him and said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿O you who are covered﴾" [i.e., the surah of al-Muddaththir].
Al-Bazzar said, after relating it through the route of Mu'alla ibn Abd al-Rahman: "Mu'alla has been narrated from by a group of people of knowledge and they accepted his narrations, but when he alone transmits hadiths, they are not followed in them."
Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I spent the night with my maternal aunt Maymunah. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray at night, and he prayed thirteen rak'ahs, among them the two rak'ahs of Fajr. I estimated his standing in each rak'ah to be about the length of [reciting] ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ — its origin is al-mutazammil, so the ta' is assimilated into the zay, and tazammul means wrapping oneself in a garment.
The majority read al-muzzammil with assimilation (idgham).
Ubayy read al-mutazammil, in its original form.
Ikrimah read it with the zay lightened, and a line like this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"As if Thabir, in the folds of its rain-clouds, were an old man wrapped in a cave-dwelling."
This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and its meaning has been disputed.
A group said: he (ﷺ) used to wrap himself in his garments at the beginning, when Jibril brought him the revelation, out of fear, until he became at ease with it. It was also said the meaning is: O you who are wrapped up with prophethood, and committed to the message.
Ikrimah said this, and he used to read "yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil" with the zay lightened and the mim with a fatha and shadda, as a passive participle. It was also said the meaning is: O you who are wrapped up in the Qur'an.
Al-Dahhak said: he wrapped himself in his garments for sleep. It was also said: word of harm from the polytheists reached him, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself, and then ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ and ﴿O you who are covered﴾ were revealed.
It is established that when the Prophet (ﷺ) heard the voice of the angel and looked at him, trembling seized him, and he came to his family and said: "Wrap me up, cover me up!" His address (ﷺ) with this form was at the beginning of the revelation's descent.
After that he was addressed with prophethood and the message.

﴿Stand [in prayer] during the night, except a little﴾: i.e., stand up for prayer at night.
The majority read qum with a kasra on the mim, due to the meeting of two sukuns.
Abu al-Simmak read it with a damma, following the damma of the qaf.
Uthman ibn Jinni said: the purpose of this vowel is to avoid the meeting of two sukuns, so whichever vowel you move it with, the purpose is achieved.
The accusative of al-layl (the night) is as an adverb of time.
It was also said that the meaning of qum is ṣalli (pray), expressed by it and used metaphorically for it.
It has been disputed whether this standing he was commanded to was obligatory for him or voluntary; what has been reported on that will come, God willing.
His saying: "except a little" is an exception from "the night": i.e., pray the whole night except a small part of it. "A little" of a thing is what is less than half; it was also said less than a sixth; it was also said less than a tenth.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: what is meant by "a little" here is a third.
This disagreement is made unnecessary by His saying: "half of it" etc. The accusative of "half of it" is as a substitute (badal) for "the night".
Al-Zajjaj said: "half of it" is a substitute for "the night", and "except a little" is an exception from "the half", and the pronoun in "from it" and "upon it" refers to the half.
The meaning: stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little to a third, or add to it a little to two-thirds; so it is as if he said: stand two-thirds of the night, or its half, or its third.
It was also said that "half of it" is a substitute for "a little". Then the meaning would be: stand the night except half of it, or less than half of it, or more than half of it. Al-Akhfash said: "half of it" means "or half of it", just as one says: give him a dirham, two dirhams, three, meaning "or two dirhams, or three."
Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: reduce from the half a little to a third, or add to the half up to two-thirds. He was given latitude in the duration of his standing in the night and was given the choice of these periods for standing. The Prophet (ﷺ) and a group with him used to stand in these measures, and it was hard on them, so a man did not know how much he had prayed or how much of the night remained, and he would stand the whole night, until Allah lightened it for them.
It was also said that the two pronouns in "from it" and "upon it" refer to the lesser part of the half, as if he said: stand less than half of it, or stand less than that lesser part, or slightly more than it. This is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that "half of it" is a substitute for "a little", and the two pronouns refer to the half that is substituted for "a little".
The abrogating element of this command has been disputed. It was said it is His saying: "Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it" to the end of the surah. It was said it is His saying: "He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it." It was said it is His saying: "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill." It was said it is abrogated by the five daily prayers; this was said by Muqatil, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Kaysan. It was said it is His saying: "So recite what is easy of it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin held that night prayer is obligatory on every Muslim, even the amount of milking a sheep.

﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured tones﴾: i.e., recite it slowly, with reflection.
Al-Dahhak said: recite it letter by letter.
Al-Zajjaj said: it is that one makes clear all the letters and gives each its due extension.
The origin of tartil is arrangement, orderliness and good sequence; and emphasizing the verb with the verbal noun indicates intensity, in a manner in which some letters are not confused with others, and nothing is lost from the pronunciation of a letter from its known point of articulation, while fully observing its prescribed vowel.

﴿Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word﴾: i.e., We will reveal to you the Qur'an, which is a weighty word.
Qatadah said: by Allah, weighty are its obligations and its limits.
Mujahid said: its lawful and its unlawful.
Al-Hasan said: acting upon it.
Abu al-Aliyah said: weighty with the promise and the threat, and the lawful and the unlawful.
Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "weighty" in the sense of noble, from the saying "so-and-so is weighty upon me," i.e., he is honored by me.
Al-Farra' said: weighty, firm, not light and trivial, because it is the speech of our Lord.
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: weighty, which none can bear except a heart supported by success and a soul adorned with monotheism. It was also said that describing it as weighty is literal, because it is established that when the Prophet (ﷺ) received revelation while on his she-camel, she would lay her chest on the ground and could not move until it had passed from him.

﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾: i.e., its hours and its times, because they arise one after another. It is said: "the thing arose" (nasha'a yansha'u) when it began and came one thing after another, so it is nashi'; and Allah brought it into being and it arose; from it: "the clouds arose" when they began. So nashi'ah is the feminine active participle of nasha'a yansha'u, so it is nashi'ah.
Al-Zajjaj said: the rising of the night is every part of it that arises, i.e., comes into being; so it is nashi'ah. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: the whole night is nashi'ah, and what is meant is that the hours of the night are the arising ones, so the descriptive is used in place of the noun described.
It was also said that the rising of the night is the soul that rises from its bed to worship, i.e., gets up, from "nasha'a min makanihi" when he rose from his place.
It was said: "nashi'ah" in Abyssinian means the standing at night. It was also said: the term nā'ishah for the standing at night is used only when it is after sleep.
Ibn al-A'rabi said: if you sleep from the beginning of the night and then rise, that is al-munsha'ah and al-nash'ah, and from it "rising of the night."
It was also said: the rising of the night is what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha', because the meaning of nasha'a is "began," and from it is the saying of Nusayb:
"Were it not that it would be said that Nusayb is childish, I would have said: 'I give myself for the young children (al-nash')'."
Ikrimah and Ata' said: the rising of the night is the beginning of the night.
Mujahid and others said: it is in the whole night, because it arises after the day; Malik chose this.
Ibn Kaysan said: it is standing at the end of the night.
Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: nā'ishat al-layl is the first of its hours.
Al-Hasan said: it is what comes after the late 'Isha' until dawn.

﴿It is more severe in treading﴾: The majority read wath'an with a fatha on the waw and sukun on the ta', maqsura (short-vowelled). Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Mujahid, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Mughirah and Abu Haywah read wiṭ'an with a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ta', mamdud (long). Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading.
So the meaning according to the first reading is that prayer during the rising of the night is heavier on the one who prays than prayer during the day, because the night is for sleep.
Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that it is heavier on the one who prays than the hours of the day, from the Arabs' saying: "the authority's trampling (wiṭ'at al-sultan) was severe on the people," when what is required of them from it became heavy upon them; and from it His saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, make your trampling heavy upon Mudar."
The meaning according to the second reading is that it is more conducive to agreement (muwāṭa'ah), i.e., more in accord, from the saying: "I agreed with so-and-so upon such-and-such, muwāṭa'ah and wiṭā'," when I concurred with him upon it.
Mujahid and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: i.e., more in agreement between hearing, sight, heart and tongue, because the sounds and movements are cut off in it. From it: "that they may make agreement with the number of what Allah has forbidden" [al-Tawbah 37], i.e., that they may agree.
al-Akhfash said: more severe in standing.
al-Farra' said: i.e., more firm for the work, and more lasting for one who wishes to increase in worship, because night is the time free from occupation with livelihood, so his worship lasts and is not cut off.
al-Kalbi said: more energetic.

﴿And more upright in speech﴾: i.e., more firm in speech and more stable in recitation, because the heart is present in it and the sounds are calm, and more upright and continuous in rightness; because the sounds in it are quiet and the world is still, so what he recites does not get confused for the one praying.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: i.e., more correct for recitation and more firm for speech, because it is a time of understanding.
Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "more upright in speech": i.e., more upright because of the freedom of mind at night.
al-Kalbi said: i.e., clearer in speech with the Qur'an.
Ikrimah said: i.e., more complete in energy and sincerity and greater in blessing.
Ibn Zayd said: more fitting that one should gain understanding of the Qur'an. It was also said: quicker in answering supplication.

﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation﴾: The majority read sabḥan with the unpointed ḥā': i.e., movement in your needs, coming and going, departing and arriving; al-sabḥ is running and circling, and from it swimming in water, because of the turning of the body and legs; and a swift horse is sābiḥ, i.e., very fast in running.
It was also said that al-sabḥ is free time: i.e., indeed you have free time by day for your needs, so pray at night.
Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., movement, coming and going in your needs and affairs.
al-Khalil said: "indeed, for you in the day is sabḥan": i.e., sleep; and al-tasabbuḥ is stretching out.
al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: if something escapes you at night, then for you by day there is free time to make up for it.
Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Wa'il and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read sabkhan with the pointed khā'. It was said the meaning of this reading is ease, spaciousness and rest.
al-Asma'i said: it is said "sabbakha Allah 'anka al-ḥummā," i.e., He lightened the fever from you; and "sabbakha al-ḥarr" means the heat abated and eased; and from it the poet's saying:
"So lighten your worry, and know that when the Most Merciful decrees something, it will be."
i.e., lighten your worry.

And tasbikh (the "sabkh" of the verse) refers to cotton that is spun after it has been carded (nadf). Al-Akhtal's verse on this is:

"They released them, scattering the dust, as the carded cotton of the bowstrings is scattered."

Tha'lab said: al-sabkh, with the unmarked kha' (sabkh), means wavering and agitation, and al-sabkh also means stillness.

Abu 'Amr said: al-sabkh means sleep and leisure.

﴿And remember the name of your Lord﴾: that is, call upon Him by His most beautiful names. It was also said: recite "in the name of your Lord" at the beginning of your prayer. It was also said: remember the name of your Lord in His promise and His threat, so that you may be keen in obedience to Him and keep far from disobeying Him. It was also said that the meaning is: persist in remembering your Lord by night and by day, and increase in that.

Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is, pray to your Lord, ﴿and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾, that is, sever yourself toward Him by devoting yourself to His worship. Tabattul means severance. One says "I battalt the thing," meaning I cut it off and separated it from other things. A "batlah" charity is one cut off from the property of its owner. A monk is called "mutabattil" because he is severed from people. On this, the poet says:

"She lights up the darkness at nightfall, as if she were
the lamp of an evening-monk, a devoted hermit."

[The verse uses] "tabtil" in place of "tabattul" for the sake of the rhyme of the verse-endings (fawasil).

Al-Wahidi said: tabattul is the renunciation of this world and all that is in it, and the seeking of what is with Allah.

﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir read "Rabb" in the genitive (jarr), as an adjective (na't) of "Rabbika," or a substitute (badal) for it, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it.

The rest read it in the nominative (raf'), either as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Lord of the East.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the accusative (nasb), as praise (mad-h).

The majority read ﴿al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib﴾ in the singular dual form, while Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb" in the plural. We have already explained the meaning of "al-mashriq wa-l-maghrib," and of "al-mashriqayn wa-l-maghribayn" and "al-mashariq wa-l-maghareb."

﴿So take Him as your trustee (wakil)﴾: that is, once you know that He alone is the One specialized in lordship, then take Him as your trustee, meaning one who manages your affairs, and rely upon Him in all of them. It was also said: take Him as your guarantor (kafil) for what He has promised you of reward and victory.

﴿And be patient over what they say﴾: of harm, abuse, and mockery, and do not be distressed by that. ﴿And keep away from them with gracious aversion﴾: that is, do not confront them, and do not occupy yourself with repaying them. It was also said that "gracious aversion" (al-hajr al-jamil) is that in which there is no distress. This was before the command to fight.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾: that is, leave them to Me, and do not concern yourself with them, for I will suffice you in their affair and take vengeance on them on your behalf.

It was said that this was revealed concerning the feeders (al-mut'imun) on the day of Badr, who were ten, and their mention has already passed.

Yahya ibn Salam said: they are the sons of al-Mughirah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: I was told they were twelve.

﴿Possessors of luxury﴾: that is, the wealthy, those of abundance, ease, and enjoyment of pleasure in this world. ﴿And give them respite a little﴾: that is, a little respite, taken as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a little time, taken as an adjective of an omitted time-noun (zaman). The meaning: give them respite until the end of their terms. It was also said: until the descent of the punishment of this world upon them, as on the day of Badr.

The first is preferable, because of His saying ﴿Indeed with Us are shackles﴾ and what follows it, for it is a threat to them of the punishment of the Hereafter. Ankal is the plural of nakl, which is a fetter. So said al-Hasan, Mujahid and others. Al-Kalbi said: al-ankal are shackles (aghlal). The first is better known in the language. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"They came to you, and their shackles were cut,
though before you they had never been cut."

Muqatil said: they are kinds of severe punishment.

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: they are fetters that cannot be undone, and a blazing fire (jahim), that is, a kindled fire.

﴿And food that chokes﴾: that is, it does not go down the throat, but lodges in it, so it neither goes down nor comes out.

Mujahid said: it is the zaqqum.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is the dari' (a thorny plant), as He said: ﴿They have no food except from dari'﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. He said: it is the thorn of the 'awsaj (a thorny shrub).

'Ikrimah said: it is a thorn that catches in the throat, neither going in nor coming out. The ghussah is the bone (shaja) in the throat, which is what lodges in it, of bone or something else, and its plural is ghusas. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾: that is, another kind of punishment, other than what has been mentioned.

﴿On the day the earth and the mountains quake﴾: the accusative of the time-phrase (zarf) is either governed by "dharni" (leave Me), or by the "being established" (istiqrar) that is related to "ladayna" (with Us), or it is an adjective of "'adhaban" (punishment), so it is attached to an omitted element: that is, a punishment occurring on the day of quaking; or it is attached to "alimam" (painful).

The majority read "turjifu" with a fatha on the ta' and damma on the jim, in the active voice. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the passive voice, derived from "arjafaha" (he made it quake), and the meaning is: it shakes and convulses with those upon it. Al-rajfah is the earthquake and the violent trembling.

﴿And the mountains will be a heap of sand, poured out﴾: that is, and the mountains will be. He expressed it in the past tense because of the certainty of its occurrence. Kathib is the gathered sand, and mahil is that which passes beneath the feet.

Al-Wahidi said: that is, flowing sand. It is said of anything you release as dust or food, "ahaltuhu hailan" (I poured it out).

Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: mahil is that which, when you step on it with the foot, slips away beneath it, and when you take its base, it collapses. On this, Hassan says:

"I recognized the abodes of Zaynab in the sand-heap,
like the writing of revelation on fresh paper."

﴿Indeed We have sent to you a messenger, a witness over you﴾: the address is to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to all disbelievers. The messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning: he will bear witness against you on the Day of Resurrection concerning your deeds. ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾: meaning Musa.

﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ whom We had sent to him, and he denied him and did not believe in what he brought. The place (mahall) of the kaf (as) is accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The meaning: Indeed We sent to you a messenger, and you disobeyed him, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger, and he disobeyed him.

﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizure﴾: that is, severe, heavy, and harsh. The meaning: We punished Pharaoh with a severe and harsh punishment by drowning. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah, that the same kind of punishment that came upon him will come upon them, even though the type of punishment differs.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, heavy and harsh; from this, rain is called "wabil" (heavy rain).

Al-Akhfash said: severe. The meanings are close. From it comes "ta'am wabil" (heavy food), meaning food that is not digestible. On this, al-Khansa' says:

"Bujaylah ate, on the day they met
the knights of Malik, a heavy eating."

﴿Then how will you guard yourselves﴾: that is, how will you protect yourselves if you disbelieve, that is, if you remain upon your disbelief, on a day, that is, the punishment of a day ﴿that will make children grey-haired﴾, because of its terrible severity. That is, the children will become old men. Shayb is the plural of ashyab. This may be literal, that they will actually become so, or figurative, because whoever witnesses a great terror has his strength diminished, his limbs weakened, and becomes like an old man in weakness and loss of power. In this there is a severe rebuke for them and a great reproach.

Al-Hasan said: that is, how will you guard yourselves against a day that will make children grey-haired if you disbelieve? Ibn Mas'ud and 'Atiyyah also read it so, with "yawman" as an object (maf'ul bih) of "tattaqun" (you guard against).

Ibn al-Anbari said: some have put "al-yawm" in the accusative governed by "kafartum" (you disbelieved), but this is ugly (qabih).

"Al-wildan" means the children.

Then He increased the description of that day in severity, saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder thereby﴾: that is, split open by it because of its severity and great terror. The clause is another adjective of "yawm." The ba' is causal (sababiyyah). It was said it means "in," that is, splitting open in it; and it was said it means "for," that is, splitting open for it. He said "munfatir" and not "munfatirah" (feminine) because the heaven is treated as a thing, since it has changed, and nothing remains of it except what is expressed as "a thing."

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: He did not say "munfatirah" because its figurative meaning (majaz) is the roof, as the poet said:

"Even if a people were raised to it (the heaven),
we would reach the heaven and the clouds."

So this is like His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected roof﴾.

Al-Farra' said: the heaven is both masculine and feminine.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is of the type of "scattered locusts" and "green tree," and [of the verse] ﴿trunks of uprooted palms﴾ [al-Qamar: 20]. He also said: that is, the heaven possesses splitting, like their saying "a woman who is murdid (nursing)": that is, one possessed of nursing, by way of attribution. Its splitting is for the descent of the angels, as He said: ﴿When the heaven is split apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], and His saying: ﴿The heavens are about to be split open from above them﴾.

It was also said "munfatir bihi" means: by Allah, and the intended meaning is by His command. The first is preferable.

﴿His promise was ever fulfilled﴾: that is, the promise of Allah regarding what He promised of resurrection, reckoning, and other things, was certain to occur without doubt. The verbal noun (masdar) is then attached to its agent (fa'il). Or it means: the promise of the day was fulfilled, and then the verbal noun is attached to its object (maf'ul).

Muqatil said: His promise was that He would make His religion prevail over all religion.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Muhammad ibn Nasr in the Book of Prayer, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Sa'd ibn Hisham, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: Tell me about the night prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: Do you not recite this surah, 'O you who wraps himself' (al-Muzzammil)? I said: Yes. She said: Indeed Allah made the night prayer obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions stood in prayer for a year, until their feet swelled. And Allah held back its conclusion in the heaven for twelve months. Then He sent down the relief at the end of this surah, and the night prayer became voluntary after it had been obligatory."

This hadith has been related from her through several chains.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the beginning of al-Muzzammil was revealed, they used to stand in prayer about as much as they stood in Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and there was about a year between its beginning and its end.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Nasr have related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: When "O you who wraps himself" was revealed, they stood for a year until their feet and shins swelled, until ﴿so recite what is easy of it﴾ was revealed, and the people rested.
